title: Flash-Radiomics: A Scalable Hybrid CPU-CUDA Engine for Standardized Scalar Radiomics and Accelerated Spatial Mapping
summary: Background and Objectives: Spatial mapping retains the spatial distribution of radiomic features, but computational cost and fragmented software limit its use. We developed Flash-Radiomics with scalar extraction and spatial mapping, a central processing unit (CPU) backend, a hybrid Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) backend, consistent feature names, and Hierarchical Data Format version 5 (HDF5) storage. Methods: We evaluated Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) compliance, CPU-CUDA concordance, and end-to-end processing time. Compliance testing included 825 chapter 1 (IBSI-1) tests covering 165 high-consensus features and 323 chapter 2 (IBSI-2) tests with numerical references. Concordance testing included 1,148 scalar pairs and 93 spatial-map pairs. End-to-end processing time was measured five times per input volume of interest (VOI) size. Comparisons included the Medical Image Radiomics Processor (MIRP) and PyRadiomics for 102 shared scalar features and PyRadiomics for 93 shared spatial maps. Results: Both backends passed all 1,148 IBSI tests, and all paired results were concordant. At the largest scalar input, CPU required 76.343 s and hybrid CUDA 81.915 s; CPU was 4.7 times faster than MIRP and 190.7 times faster than PyRadiomics. At the largest spatial input completed by both backends, hybrid CUDA reduced processing time by 68.6% relative to CPU (79.280 versus 252.791 s). At PyRadiomics' largest completed spatial input, hybrid CUDA was 84.9 times faster. Conclusions: Flash-Radiomics unified standardized scalar extraction, spatial mapping, concordant CPU-CUDA results, and HDF5 storage. CPU processing time was similar or shorter for scalar extraction, whereas hybrid CUDA was faster for spatial mapping under the tested conditions.

AI.tldr: Flash-Radiomics is a new radiomics tool with CPU and hybrid CUDA backends, providing scalar extraction and spatial mapping with IBSI compliance, concordant results across backends, HDF5 storage, and significant speed advantages over MIRP and PyRadiomics.
AI.motivation: Spatial mapping preserves the spatial distribution of radiomic features, but its use is limited by high computational cost and fragmented software. There is a need for a unified tool that is both standardized and computationally efficient.
AI.method: The authors developed Flash-Radiomics with scalar extraction and spatial mapping, a CPU backend, a hybrid CUDA backend, consistent feature names, and HDF5 storage. They evaluated IBSI compliance (825 IBSI-1 tests, 323 IBSI-2 tests), CPU-CUDA concordance (1,148 scalar pairs, 93 spatial-map pairs), and end-to-end processing time across VOI sizes, comparing against MIRP and PyRadiomics.
AI.result: Both backends passed all 1,148 IBSI tests with concordant paired results. At the largest scalar input, CPU took 76.343 s vs hybrid CUDA 81.915 s; CPU was 4.7x faster than MIRP and 190.7x faster than PyRadiomics. At the largest spatial input, hybrid CUDA reduced time by 68.6% over CPU (79.280 vs 252.791 s) and was 84.9x faster than PyRadiomics at its largest completed spatial input.
AI.conclusion: Flash-Radiomics unifies standardized scalar extraction, spatial mapping, concordant CPU-CUDA results, and HDF5 storage. CPU was similar or faster for scalar extraction, while hybrid CUDA was faster for spatial mapping under tested conditions.

title: A Combined ODE Model of Carbohydrate Fermentation and Colorectal Cancer
summary: We formulate and analyze a system of non-linear ordinary differential equations that describe key metabolic and immunological interactions between butyrate produced by fiber-fermenting gut microbiota, colorectal cancer cells and host cell populations. The model is studied both independently and in conjunction with a pre-existing carbohydrate fermentation model. The parameter space is explored through sensitivity analyses. Simulation experiments are conducted to illustrate the emergence of varying dynamical behaviour driven by butyrate availability. Our model predicts that butyrate production is driven by fiber consumption and further supported by probiotics in the case of microbial dysbiosis. It also suggests that butyrate may help in suppressing tumour growth. We also show that by adding noise with sufficiently high intensity, cancer elimination occurs almost surely in infinite time and that this threshold level of noise intensity decreases with increasing butyrate concentrations.

AI.tldr: A nonlinear ODE model links butyrate from fiber-fermenting gut microbiota to colorectal cancer cells and host cell populations, showing butyrate suppresses tumour growth and that sufficiently intense noise yields almost-sure cancer elimination.
AI.motivation: To understand the metabolic and immunological interactions between butyrate-producing gut microbiota, colorectal cancer cells, and host cells, given the role of fiber fermentation and microbial dysbiosis in cancer dynamics.
AI.method: Formulate and analyze a system of nonlinear ODEs describing butyrate, cancer cells, and host cell populations. Study the model independently and jointly with an existing carbohydrate fermentation model. Explore parameter space via sensitivity analyses and run simulation experiments under varying butyrate availability, including stochastic noise.
AI.result: Butyrate production is driven by fiber consumption and supported by probiotics under microbial dysbiosis. Butyrate may help suppress tumour growth. Adding sufficiently high-intensity noise leads to almost-sure cancer elimination in infinite time, and this noise threshold decreases as butyrate concentration increases.
AI.conclusion: The model highlights butyrate's role in limiting colorectal tumour growth and shows that stochastic effects can guarantee cancer elimination, with higher butyrate lowering the required noise intensity.

title: Large Language Model Agents for Evidence Based Genetic Disease Severity Classification
summary: Disease severity classification for genetic conditions is subjective and labor-intensive, creating bottlenecks in genomic screening, where commercial panels vary widely in size and overlap. We developed an autonomous AI agent integrating Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to classify 10,211 Human Phenotype Ontology terms. It uses American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG)-endorsed severity guidelines and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) quality-of-life criteria to retrieve PubMed literature, generate interpretable reasoning chains, and independently verify claims. At the phenotype level, using expert-curated cohorts, the agent achieved 93.55% accuracy (MCC 0.9237) with 82.6% to 91.4% of claims supported by direct evidence or valid inferences. Gene-level severity was aggregated across 8,738 pairs, identifying 3,283 autosomal recessive pairs with severe or profound presentations. External validation showed 95.2% concordance with Mackenzie's Mission gene list. This system enables standardized panel design by providing reliable, automated classification supported by direct evidence.

AI.tldr: An autonomous ReAct+RAG AI agent classifies 10,211 HPO terms by disease severity, achieving 93.55% phenotype-level accuracy and 95.2% external concordance, enabling standardized genomic panel design.
AI.motivation: Disease severity classification for genetic conditions is subjective and labor-intensive, creating bottlenecks in genomic screening where commercial panels vary widely in size and overlap.
AI.method: Integrates ReAct reasoning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to classify 10,211 HPO terms, using ACMG-endorsed severity guidelines and ACOG quality-of-life criteria to retrieve PubMed literature, generate interpretable reasoning chains, and self-verify claims. Gene-level severity is aggregated across 8,738 pairs.
AI.result: Phenotype-level accuracy 93.55% (MCC 0.9237) with 82.6–91.4% of claims supported by direct evidence or valid inferences; 3,283 autosomal recessive pairs with severe/profound presentations identified; 95.2% concordance with Mackenzie's Mission gene list.
AI.conclusion: The system enables standardized panel design through reliable, automated severity classification supported by direct evidence.

title: Self-Replicating Neural Cellular Automata: Quantifying Emergent Phenotypic and Genotypic Diversity in an OpenEnded Substrate
summary: We study an in-silico substrate in which every pixel of a two-channel cellular-automata grid carries a tiny neural network (an agent) that senses its Moore neighborhood. A cell persists only by self-replication: a living neighbor is cloned and its weights are mutated by a uniform perturbation, so that phenotype (cell state) is driven entirely by genotype (network weights). From a handful of seeded founders the system grows into a spatially organized ecosystem of coexisting, competing and dominating species. Our main contribution is a battery of coarse-grained diversity metrics that make such growth measurable at two scales: four phenotypic tools based on cellular-type frequency, entropy and cell variance, and two genotypic tools that colour each agent by a hash of its full weight vector versus a sparse random-weight probe. Across a five-fold sweep of 1680 small runs and 24 long (1000-generation, 200 x 200) runs, the substrate is persistent and self-maintaining in 20 of the 24 long configurations and exposes a clear phenotype-genotype diversity trade-off: raising phenotypic diversity collapses genotypic diversity and vice versa. Full-genome hash colouring further reveals lineage structure that a random-weight probe systematically misses. Code, data and animations are released as supplementary material.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a cellular-automata substrate where each pixel hosts a tiny neural network agent that replicates via cloning with mutation, and introduces coarse-grained diversity metrics to measure the resulting ecosystem at phenotypic and genotypic scales.
AI.motivation: Growth of self-replicating neural agents in a spatial substrate is hard to measure in terms of diversity; the authors want metrics that capture ecosystem organization at multiple scales.
AI.method: A two-channel cellular-automata grid where each cell contains a small neural network sensing its Moore neighborhood. Cells persist only by self-replication: a living neighbor is cloned and its weights mutated by uniform perturbation, so phenotype (cell state) is driven by genotype (weights). Four phenotypic metrics (cell-type frequency, entropy, cell variance) and two genotypic metrics (full-weight-vector hash coloring vs. sparse random-weight probe) are evaluated over 1680 small runs (five-fold sweep) and 24 long runs (1000 generations, 200x200).
AI.result: The substrate is persistent and self-maintaining in 20 of 24 long configurations, forming spatially organized ecosystems of coexisting, competing, and dominating species. A clear phenotype-genotype diversity trade-off emerges: raising phenotypic diversity collapses genotypic diversity and vice versa. Full-genome hash coloring reveals lineage structure that the random-weight probe systematically misses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed coarse-grained diversity metrics successfully make growth measurable at two scales, expose a phenotype-genotype diversity trade-off, and show that full-genome coloring captures lineage structure better than sparse probes. Code, data, and animations are released as supplementary material.

title: A Mathematical Model of Motivated Emotional Mind - Cognitive Embodied System
summary: This article presents a mathematical model of the Motivated Emotional Mind cognitive architecture developed for embodied intelligent systems. Such a system learns to maintain its homeostasis through a generalized form of reinforcement learning based on its internal motivations, termed motivated learning (ML). The principal contribution of this article is a rigorous formalization of the re-entrant loop integrating feedforward processing, lateral interactions, and feedback pathways, together with the representational selection mechanisms that govern adaptive system responses. The model specifies how ongoing exteroceptive and interoceptive signals, bodily-motivational context, and memory traces are bound into associative memory structures termed semblions, which compete for access to further processing and top-down reconstruction. The formalization encompasses secondary perception, representational competition, curiosity, procedural gaps, and action selection directed toward limiting allostatic violations. Within this framework, motivated learning is tailored to embodied systems whose dynamics are shaped by needs, affect, and the current regulatory state. Unlike standard reinforcement-learning models, the proposed approach incorporates need thresholds, goal generation and shifting goals, bodily state, resource constraints, and action uncertainty, thereby providing a more adequate account of response selection under regulatory pressure. Global affect functions as a central control signal, modulating the learning rate, representational valence, and the balance between exploration and exploitation. The model presented here is a step toward a more rigorous formalization of cognitive phenomena and may provide a basis for further theoretical analysis, computer simulation, and implementation in artificial-intelligence systems inspired by biological processes.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes a "Motivated Emotional Mind" cognitive architecture using motivated learning (ML), a generalized reinforcement-learning approach that maintains homeostasis in embodied systems through internal motivations, needs, and affect.
AI.motivation: Standard reinforcement-learning models inadequately capture how embodied agents select responses under regulatory pressure, since they neglect need thresholds, goal generation/shifting, bodily state, resource constraints, and action uncertainty.
AI.method: A mathematical model is developed to formalize a re-entrant loop integrating feedforward processing, lateral interactions, and feedback pathways, plus representational selection mechanisms. Exteroceptive/interoceptive signals, bodily-motivational context, and memory traces bind into associative memory structures called "semblions," which compete for further processing and top-down reconstruction. The formalization covers secondary perception, representational competition, curiosity, procedural gaps, and action selection aimed at limiting allostatic violations. Global affect acts as a central control signal modulating learning rate, representational valence, and the exploration-exploitation balance.
AI.result: The framework yields a rigorous formalization of motivated learning tailored to embodied systems whose dynamics are shaped by needs, affect, and regulatory state, providing a more adequate account of response selection than standard RL.
AI.conclusion: This work is a step toward rigorous formalization of cognitive phenomena and may serve as a basis for further theoretical analysis, computer simulation, and implementation in biologically inspired AI systems.

title: When AI Generates Covariates: Causal Typing and Estimand Drift in Sequential Experiments
comment: 29 pages. Ancillary files include simulation code, seeds, and replicate-level results
summary:
AI-generated covariates from notes, conversations, images, and wearable streams can change the causal question when their roles are left unspecified. A generated feature may represent a treatment version, pre-action state, history, design variable, mediator, outcome proxy, observation process, or intercurrent event; these roles are not interchangeable.
  We formulate a causal type discipline for sequential experiments: a versioned representation map, a causal role classifier, a claim-status filter, and an estimand lock. The lock fixes a standardized proximal effect before generated covariates enter the analysis. Under audit correctness and standard identification assumptions, admissible role assignments preserve this estimand. We apply the established conditional-covariance characterization of compression bias to substitution of generated representations for design-relevant states. A standardized decomposition separates compression, conditional-law, and standardization drift. Further results cover mediator adjustment, post-action leakage, marker-intervention conflation, outcome-guided discovery, and state-measurement error. Cluster-level orthogonal estimators distinguish empirical and superpopulation targets under repeated sessions and missing outcomes.
  Simulations show that refinement helps when it retains design-relevant information, whereas design erasure, leakage, and same-data marker selection can produce bias or undercoverage. The framework places causal semantics and claim status before confirmatory inference with generated representations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a causal type discipline for using AI-generated covariates in sequential experiments, ensuring that the causal estimand is fixed and preserved regardless of how generated features are assigned roles.
AI.motivation: AI-generated covariates (from notes, conversations, images, wearable streams) can inadvertently change the causal question when their roles are ambiguous, since a generated feature may serve as a treatment version, pre-action state, history, design variable, mediator, outcome proxy, observation process, or intercurrent event.
AI.method: The authors formulate a causal type discipline with four components: a versioned representation map, a causal role classifier, a claim-status filter, and an estimand lock that fixes a standardized proximal effect before generated covariates enter analysis. They apply a conditional-covariance characterization of compression bias, derive a standardized decomposition separating compression, conditional-law, and standardization drift, and extend results to mediator adjustment, post-action leakage, marker-intervention conflation, outcome-guided discovery, and state-measurement error, with cluster-level orthogonal estimators distinguishing empirical and superpopulation targets.
AI.result: Admissible role assignments preserve the locked estimand under audit correctness and standard identification assumptions. Simulations show refinement helps when it retains design-relevant information, while design erasure, leakage, and same-data marker selection can cause bias or undercoverage.
AI.conclusion: The framework places causal semantics and claim status before confirmatory inference when using generated representations.

title: BioPhys-Bridge: A Benchmark for Interdisciplinary Scientific Reasoning in Physics-Grounded Biological Research
comment: Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2026, 11 pages, 3 figures
summary: Language models face unique challenges in analyzing interdisciplinary scientific research literature. In biophysics research, faithful answers require grounding observed data in source evidence, interpreting it through a quantitative physics model, and linking it to a biological mechanism. To address this challenge, we introduce BioPhys-Bridge, a novel benchmark dataset for evidence-grounded scientific reasoning over biophysical literature. Each case contains evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets for question answering (QA) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The initial release contains 500 cases, 1,517 agent-facing tasks, and covers six biological domains and nine physical model families, including three sparse families reserved for future expansion. We enforce strict quality gates for all cases in schema, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, source-license, duplicate, unit-normalization, with domain expert review and annotation for 81 cases. Preliminary evaluations show that DeepSeek-V4-Flash obtain the highest evidence-ID $F_1$ score (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294). BioPhys-Bridge is an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design with complex, multi-step scientific reasoning. Future works will increase the size and complexity of the dataset and perform comprehensive evaluations. Code and data are available in the GitHub repository and on Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: BioPhys-Bridge is a new benchmark dataset for evidence-grounded scientific reasoning over biophysical literature, containing 500 cases and 1,517 tasks, with preliminary model evaluations.
AI.motivation: Language models struggle with interdisciplinary scientific literature. In biophysics, faithful answers require grounding data in source evidence, interpreting it via quantitative physics models, and linking it to biological mechanisms—capabilities current models lack.
AI.method: The authors built BioPhys-Bridge, where each case includes evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets for QA and RAG. Initial release has 500 cases, 1,517 agent-facing tasks, six biological domains, nine physical model families (three sparse, reserved for expansion), and strict quality gates plus expert review of 81 cases.
AI.result: Preliminary evaluations show DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieves the highest evidence-ID F1 (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294), indicating modest performance.
AI.conclusion: BioPhys-Bridge serves as an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design via complex multi-step reasoning. Future work will expand dataset size/complexity and conduct comprehensive evaluations. Code and data are publicly available.

title: "I Know Where to Look," But Does the LLM? Charting the Gaps Between Clinical Expert Needs and Unstructured Data Abstraction Tools
summary: Clinical data abstraction, the process of distilling structured information from patient records, plays a key role in advancing knowledge about diseases such as cancer. Information extraction (IE) with large language models (LLMs) could accelerate this process, but it is unclear whether current frameworks effectively support clinical researchers without AI expertise. To address this, we co-designed an interactive LLM-based abstraction system called Libretto with seven cancer research teams, then evaluated the system's ability to help them answer real-world research questions. We found that while clinicians knew where and how to annotate complex concepts in patient notes, in twelve of fourteen tasks they faced barriers to replicating those intuitions with LLMs. Contextual note reliability judgments, difficulties in steering vibe-coded prompts, and inflexible evaluation strategies necessitated fundamental changes to the IE workflow. Our results highlight open problems for HCI research to bridge the gaps between AI data work tools and clinical users' needs.

AI.tldr: Libretto is a co-designed interactive LLM-based abstraction system that helps cancer researchers extract structured data from patient records, but evaluation with seven teams reveals that clinicians struggle to translate their annotation intuitions into effective LLM prompts and evaluations.
AI.motivation: Clinical data abstraction is critical for advancing disease knowledge such as cancer, and LLM-based information extraction could accelerate it. However, it is unclear whether current frameworks effectively support clinical researchers who lack AI expertise.
AI.method: Co-designed an interactive LLM-based abstraction system called Libretto with seven cancer research teams, then evaluated its ability to help them answer real-world research questions.
AI.result: Clinicians knew where and how to annotate complex concepts in patient notes, but in twelve of fourteen tasks they faced barriers replicating those intuitions with LLMs. Key challenges included contextual note reliability judgments, difficulty steering vibe-coded prompts, and inflexible evaluation strategies, necessitating fundamental changes to the IE workflow.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights open problems for HCI research to bridge the gaps between AI data work tools and clinical users' needs.

title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) Improves Classification Accuracy of Bacterial Raman Spectral Data Enabling Portable Diagnostics
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at the ICLR 2024 Workshop on Practical ML for Low Resource Settings (PML4LRS)
summary: Antimicrobial resistance is expected to claim 10 million lives per year by 2050, and resource-limited regions are most affected. Raman spectroscopy is a novel pathogen diagnostic approach promising rapid and portable antibiotic resistance testing within a few hours, compared to days when using gold standard methods. However, current algorithms for Raman spectra analysis 1) are unable to generalize well on limited datasets across diverse patient populations and 2) require increased complexity due to the necessity of non-trivial pre-processing steps, such as feature extraction, which are essential to mitigate the low-quality nature of Raman spectral data. In this work, we address these limitations using Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to enhance model generalization across a diverse array of hyperparameters in clinical bacterial isolate classification tasks. We demonstrate that SAM achieves accuracy improvements of up to 10.5% on a single split, and an increase in average accuracy of 2.7% across all splits in spectral classification tasks over the traditional optimizer, Adam. These results display the capability of SAM to advance the clinical application of AI-powered Raman spectroscopy tools.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to improve generalization of Raman spectroscopy-based pathogen classification for antibiotic resistance testing.
AI.motivation: Antimicrobial resistance threatens 10 million lives annually by 2050, especially in resource-limited regions. Raman spectroscopy enables rapid, portable antibiotic resistance testing, but current algorithms generalize poorly on limited datasets across diverse populations and require complex pre-processing to handle low-quality spectral data.
AI.method: The authors use Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to enhance model generalization across a diverse array of hyperparameters in clinical bacterial isolate classification tasks.
AI.result: SAM achieves up to 10.5% accuracy improvement on a single split and a 2.7% increase in average accuracy across all splits over the traditional optimizer Adam in spectral classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: SAM can advance the clinical application of AI-powered Raman spectroscopy tools by improving generalization in antibiotic resistance testing.

title: T2 estimation from MOLLI acquisitions
summary: Cardiac T1 and T2 quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a technique that provides characterization of a multitude of myocardial pathologies. However, each parameter requires its own specialized acquisition sequence, which may be time-consuming. In this work, we demonstrate that MOLLI, an acquisition sequence commonly used to perform T1 mapping, is also sensitive to T2, and can also be used for myocardial T2 mapping. Although MOLLI is not designed for T2 mapping, its signal evolution inherently depends on both T1 and T2 relaxation. Here, we demonstrate that this dependence is sufficiently strong to allow T2 estimation directly from MOLLI T1-weighted images, using appropriate signal modelling. This finding opens the possibility of obtaining simultaneously T1 and T2 maps from a single MOLLI acquisition, reducing total scan time and potentially improving patient comfort and clinical throughput.

AI.tldr: MOLLI, a sequence normally used for cardiac T1 mapping, is also sensitive to T2 and can be used to obtain simultaneous T1 and T2 maps from a single acquisition.
AI.motivation: Cardiac T1 and T2 quantitative MRI characterizes myocardial pathologies, but each parameter requires its own specialized acquisition sequence, making scans time-consuming.
AI.method: The authors show that MOLLI's signal evolution inherently depends on both T1 and T2 relaxation, and that this dependence is strong enough to estimate T2 directly from MOLLI T1-weighted images using appropriate signal modelling.
AI.result: T2 can be estimated directly from MOLLI T1-weighted images, despite MOLLI not being designed for T2 mapping.
AI.conclusion: This enables simultaneous T1 and T2 maps from a single MOLLI acquisition, reducing total scan time and potentially improving patient comfort and clinical throughput.

title: Dynamic Generalized Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport
summary: Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) extends classical optimal transport by introducing structure-aware transport cost. This is particularly relevant for spatial transcriptomics, where dynamical reconstruction should preserve tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns. While static formulations have been widely used for such structure-aware alignment, a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is still missing. We introduce Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE), a theoretical and computational framework to generalize GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner. We formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove the static dynamic equivalence. We further develop travelling-pair flow matching, which allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes their interactions into a single vector field. On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

AI.tldr: TP-DATE generalizes Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport to a dynamic, simulation-free framework via travelling-pair flow matching, improving spatial structure preservation and 3D dynamics reconstruction in spatial transcriptomics.
AI.motivation: GW-OT adds structure-aware cost to classical OT, valuable for spatial transcriptomics where reconstruction must preserve tissue structure while matching expression. Static formulations dominate, but a general dynamic formulation for continuous trajectory reconstruction is missing.
AI.method: They formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove static-dynamic equivalence. They then develop travelling-pair flow matching, enabling interacting conditional paths and marginalizing their interactions into a single vector field, yielding a simulation-free dynamic GW-OT framework.
AI.result: On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: TP-DATE provides a theoretical and computational framework generalizing GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner, advancing structure-aware dynamical reconstruction.

title: Intact-to-Amputee Transfer in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding: Training Source and Calibration Budget
summary: A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A systematic review of 1077 studies quantifies where the evidence is thin: amputees appear in about one in six. Here a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder is carried to eleven transradial amputees on a protocol matched to its intact-limb training data. Zero-shot cross-population transfer fails outright: the encoder requires labeled data from the new user before it begins decoding, and it then exceeds the per-user classifier a clinic would fit by 0.190 macro F1 at three repetitions and for every subject in the cohort. Given three labelled repetitions it reaches 0.779 macro-F1 against 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on forty intact subjects produces better transfers to a new amputee than training on ten other amputees, and combining the two produces better transfers than either individually. The prediction pre-registered for this study, which extends the encoder's baseline-strength account with the premise that amputee EMG is less separable, holds true only after a few repetitions become available and after enriching the source pool with additional amputees. At a single repetition, and at every budget under a source matched to the intact-limb comparison, it fails. Thus, it locates the boundary of the proposed account.

AI.tldr: A montage-agnostic cross-user EMG encoder fails zero-shot transfer to amputees but outperforms per-user classifiers once a few labeled repetitions are available, and transfer improves by combining intact-limb and amputee training data.
AI.motivation: Myoelectric recognisers trained on one person rarely transfer to another, and clinical use typically requires fresh labeled calibration per end user. Evidence on amputees is thin—only about one in six of 1077 reviewed studies include them—so it is unclear whether cross-user encoders transfer across populations.
AI.method: A montage-agnostic cross-user encoder is evaluated on eleven transradial amputees under a protocol matched to its intact-limb training data. Source pools vary (40 intact subjects vs. 10 amputees vs. combined), and performance is measured as a function of labeled repetitions from the new user.
AI.result: Zero-shot cross-population transfer fails outright; the encoder needs labeled data from the new user. With three labeled repetitions it reaches 0.779 macro-F1 vs. 0.589 for a per-user pipeline, exceeding it by 0.190 and for every subject. Training on 40 intact subjects transfers better than training on 10 amputees, and combining both is best. The pre-registered prediction holds only after a few repetitions and after enriching the source pool with amputees; at a single repetition it fails.
AI.conclusion: The baseline-strength account extended with a "less separable amputee EMG" premise is only partially supported, locating its boundary at low calibration budgets. Cross-user transfer to amputees is feasible but not zero-shot.
